strengths: MUSplat presents a coherent and potentially useful pipeline for adding open-vocabulary semantics to an existing 3DGS scene without additional semantic optimization. Tracked masks, rendering-weight-based lifting, boundary filtering, and VLM-generated descriptions fit together naturally.

The reported results are competitive across two relevant tasks. On LERF, 54.3 mIoU exceeds the strongest listed point-based baseline by 10.7 points and the strongest pixel-based baseline by 2.9 points. On ScanNet, the method leads all listed baselines across the three class subsets and both metrics.

The feature-extraction ablation provides meaningful evidence for the VLM component: 54.3 mIoU versus 50.1 for filtered multi-view image features, 39.2 for averaged features, and 36.9 for single-view features.

The grouping equations are understandable, and the boundary-processing ablation shows a modest improvement from 53.0 to 54.3 mIoU. The qualitative examples also illustrate useful fine-grained selections.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not adequately measured. Table 1 reports training time as 'None' but omits runtime for SAM segmentation, DAM2SAM tracking, mask lifting, and Gemini inference. No end-to-end timings substantiate the claimed reduction from hours to minutes. Peak VRAM covers grouping only, and CLIP-feature storage excludes other pipeline assets. Eliminating semantic optimization is valuable, but these measurements do not establish the claimed overall computational advantage.

Reproducibility is materially limited. The manuscript omits the VLM prompt, number of selected views, CLIP configuration, entropy and opacity thresholds, matching threshold, detection interval, and new-instance IoU threshold. It also does not explain how overlapping class selections or excluded neutral points are handled during ScanNet scoring. Section 3.3 uses thresholded matching, whereas Section 4.1 describes selecting the most similar instances, leaving the evaluated decision rule unclear.

The headline polysemy claim receives insufficient direct evaluation. Multiple mask granularities and candidate names plausibly permit overlapping semantic associations, but there is no controlled evaluation showing that the same points support object, material, and superclass queries, nor an ablation isolating this capability. Moreover, assigning one embedding to a Gaussian does not inherently restrict it to matching one semantic concept, so the stated incapability of prior methods is not established.

The originality of matching-based mask lifting is insufficiently contextualized. Closely relevant works, including FlashSplat and Segment then Splat, appear in the bibliography but are neither substantively discussed nor compared. Consequently, the manuscript does not clearly distinguish its lifting contribution from existing segmentation-transfer approaches. The supported novelty appears primarily to lie in the combined pipeline, VLM association, and boundary heuristic.

The boundary mechanism has limited technical validation. High semantic entropy can arise from tracking errors or occlusion, while Gaussian opacity alone does not establish whether a point is a transitional boundary element or a valid surface contribution. Visibility handling for the center-projection entropy calculation is unspecified. The aggregate 1.3-point gain supports practical usefulness, but does not validate the proposed interpretation of neutral points or robustness across these cases.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence: the 10.7-point LERF improvement applies only to point-based baselines, and aggregate ScanNet results do not establish superiority in every scene. More broadly, the promising accuracy results favor the approach, but missing evaluation details and inadequate support for the central efficiency and polysemy claims currently outweigh them, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: MUSplat offers a useful pipeline for adding language-queryable object groups to an existing 3DGS reconstruction without per-scene semantic optimization. Rendering-weight-based mask lifting, tracked masks, and VLM-generated descriptions form a coherent practical approach.

The reported performance is competitive: Table 2 achieves 54.3 mIoU on LERF, exceeding the strongest listed point-based baseline by 10.7 points and the strongest pixel-based baseline by 2.9 points. Table 3 improves ScanNet mIoU over the strongest listed baseline by 4.8, 4.7, and 2.9 points for the three category settings.

The ablations provide useful component-level evidence. VLM text matching improves over filtered CLIP image matching from 50.1 to 54.3 mIoU, while neutral-point processing improves the unfiltered result from 53.0 to 54.3. Qualitative examples also illustrate successful part-level selections.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not adequately measured. Table 1 reports training time as 'None' for MUSplat, but provides no elapsed preprocessing or end-to-end adaptation time accounting for SAM, DAM2SAM tracking, mask lifting, and Gemini inference. Thus, the claimed reduction from hours to minutes is unsupported. Grouping-stage VRAM and CLIP-feature storage are useful partial measurements, but do not establish total resource savings.

Important details needed to reproduce the reported results are missing: the VLM prompt, number of selected views, generation settings, CLIP backbone, matching threshold, entropy and opacity thresholds, detection interval, and new-instance IoU threshold. The treatment of overlapping predictions and unassigned points in ScanNet evaluation is also unclear. These choices directly determine grouping and semantic predictions, making their omission consequential.

The headline polysemy claim receives little direct evaluation. Multiple descriptions and overlapping groups can support multiple concepts, but the paper does not quantify retrieval of categories, attributes, and parts for the same points or ablate the multigranularity representation. Moreover, assigning one feature vector to a Gaussian does not inherently prevent that vector from matching multiple language queries, so the asserted incapability of prior representations is too broad.

The novelty of the grouping mechanism is insufficiently situated. FlashSplat, Segment then Splat, and Tackling View-Dependent Semantics in 3D Language Gaussian Splatting appear in the bibliography but receive no substantive comparison. Their stated topics directly overlap mask lifting, segmentation-first pipelines, and viewpoint-dependent semantics. The manuscript therefore does not adequately establish what advances beyond related approaches, particularly for its broad claims about training-free 3D understanding.

The experiments support the usefulness of Gemini-generated descriptions more strongly than the proposed explanation of robust multi-view distillation. Table 5 changes both the foundation model and the representation modality; it does not compare single-view and multi-view VLM descriptions. Likewise, the assertion that downstream processing handles tracking and re-identification errors lacks a corresponding robustness experiment. For neutral-point processing, low opacity is a heuristic rather than an established indicator of semantic neutrality, and visibility/occlusion handling for the entropy calculation is insufficiently specified.

Several claims exceed the presented evidence: the 10.7-point LERF improvement applies only to point-based competitors, and aggregate ScanNet results do not establish superiority 'across all scenes.' These wording issues are readily correctable. My weak-reject recommendation instead rests on the combined lack of reproducible implementation details, measured end-to-end efficiency, and evidence establishing the central polysemy and methodological novelty claims, despite the worthwhile reported accuracy gains.

strengths: MUSplat offers a coherent, practically useful pipeline for adding open-vocabulary semantics to an existing 3DGS reconstruction without additional semantic optimization. Rendering-weighted mask lifting, tracked object groups, and VLM-generated descriptions fit together naturally.

The reported performance is promising across two tasks. On LERF, 54.3 mean IoU exceeds the strongest listed point-based baseline by 10.7 points and the strongest pixel-based baseline by 2.9 points. On ScanNet, the method improves over the listed baselines across all three class configurations, including 45.5 versus 40.7 mIoU for 19 classes.

The feature-extraction ablation provides meaningful evidence: VLM text matching achieves 54.3 mIoU versus 50.1 for filtered multi-view image matching and 39.2 for simple averaging. This supports using textual descriptions to improve retrieval in the proposed pipeline.
The method is generally understandable, with explicit mask-lifting equations and useful pipeline illustrations. The neutral-point ablation also measures a modest improvement, from 53.0 to 54.3 mIoU.
weaknesses: The main efficiency claim is not adequately measured. Table 1 reports no training for MUSplat, but omits its actual scene-adaptation time, including SAM, DAM2SAM tracking, mask lifting, and Gemini inference. Hardware, API latency/cost, and consistent timing boundaries are unspecified. Consequently, the claimed reduction from hours to minutes and overall computational advantage are not established by the presented measurements.

Essential reproduction details are missing: the entropy and opacity thresholds, retrieval threshold, number of selected views, actual VLM prompt and generation settings, CLIP variant, detection interval, and new-instance IoU threshold. The ScanNet evaluation also does not explain how overlapping class selections or unassigned points are handled. These choices directly affect the reported accuracy, making this a material experimental limitation.

The central polysemy claim is insufficiently demonstrated. Multiple candidate names and overlapping groups can support multiple descriptions, but the experiments do not isolate simultaneous category, material, attribute, and part membership for the same points. Moreover, having one embedding per Gaussian does not inherently restrict similarity matching to one semantic concept, so the asserted incapability of prior approaches is too strong.

Originality is not positioned adequately against closely related work. FlashSplat, Segment then Splat, and Tackling View-dependent Semantics appear in the bibliography but receive no substantive discussion. Their relationship to direct mask lifting and multi-view semantic aggregation needs to be established. The experiments also do not isolate the contribution of multi-granularity tracking from the benefit of introducing Gemini-generated descriptions.

The neutral-point mechanism rests on an unvalidated assumption that low-opacity, semantically inconsistent Gaussians represent transitional boundaries. Opacity is not itself a reliable surface-membership label, and point visibility for the entropy calculation is underspecified. The small aggregate gain supports the heuristic's usefulness, but not the stronger interpretation or the claim that both stages are essential.

Overall, the benchmark gains and practical integration are worthwhile. However, insufficient support for the central efficiency and polysemy claims, unclear differentiation from related methods, and consequential reproducibility omissions currently outweigh those merits, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The object-centric representation is useful and coherent: overlapping Gaussian groups support part–whole membership, while group-level textual features enable direct 3D querying without optimizing per-Gaussian semantic embeddings.

ScanNet results provide meaningful evidence of effectiveness. Table 3 reports 45.5 mIoU over 19 classes versus 40.7 for InstanceGaussian, with improvements across all three evaluated class subsets. On LERF, 54.3 mIoU exceeds LUDVIG's 50.4 among the listed training-free 3D methods.

The feature-extraction ablation supports VLM-based text distillation: Table 5 improves from 50.1 mIoU with filtered multi-view CLIP image features to 54.3 with text features. The supplementary VLM and descriptor-count comparisons further characterize this component.

The supplementary material supplies useful implementation details, prompts, threshold sweeps, failure examples, and a component-level runtime breakdown. The reported approximately nine-minute semantic adaptation pipeline suggests practical value.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claims lack comparable accounting. Table 1 reports CLIP-feature storage rather than the complete semantic representation, including overlapping Gaussian-index sets. It assigns approximately 3 GB to every feature-based baseline despite discussing compressed representations. Table 9 includes Gemini inference under timings described as measured on a V100, without specifying remote inference resources or costs. Section 8 also compares semantic adaptation from pretrained geometry with InstanceGaussian's geometry-training time. These issues prevent verification of the claimed orders-of-magnitude storage reduction and overall computational advantage.

The evidence does not isolate the proposed extrinsic architecture from stronger input models. Table 5 supports text distillation within the proposed pipeline, but there is no controlled comparison holding tracking, masks, and VLM descriptors fixed while changing the semantic representation. Nor is overlapping multi-granularity grouping ablated against single-granularity or disjoint grouping. Consequently, gains cannot be confidently attributed to the claimed new paradigm or polysemy mechanism.

The neutral-point mechanism has an implementation-significant inconsistency. Section 3.3 preserves high-entropy points when opacity exceeds the threshold, so setting the opacity threshold to zero should preserve essentially all positive-opacity candidates. Supplement Section 7.2 instead says this setting removes all high-entropy points and reports the entropy-only result. Moreover, entropy and low opacity are plausible heuristics but do not establish that selected points intrinsically lack semantic identity; tracking errors and visibility effects can also cause disagreement.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The claimed LERF state of the art and 3.9-point improvement refer only to LUDVIG: Table 2 also reports 64.0 for LAGA, 62.0 for 3DVLGS, and 61.3 for Occam's LGS, versus 54.3 for ExtrinSplat. Five generated nouns also provide limited support for broad claims about rich polysemy, nuanced attributes, and occlusion invariance. The reported overlap statistic is not an independently annotated evaluation of semantic correctness.

Reproduction remains underspecified in consequential places: the CLIP backbone, VLM decoding/version settings, visibility determination for entropy, and treatment of overlapping class predictions and unassigned points in ScanNet are not clearly documented. Overall, the measured segmentation gains and practical design place this near the acceptance boundary, but uncertainty about the headline efficiency advantage and the distinct contribution of the architecture prevents a stronger recommendation.

strengths: The object-centric representation is useful and technically coherent: overlapping Gaussian groups reference shared geometry and carry VLM-generated textual descriptions. This enables part–whole selections without storing a separate high-dimensional embedding at every Gaussian.

ScanNet results provide substantive evidence of effectiveness. Table 3 reports 45.5 mIoU for 19 classes, compared with 40.7 for InstanceGaussian and 33.9 for LUDVIG, with improvements also reported for the 15- and 10-class settings.

LERF performance offers a promising accuracy–efficiency trade-off. The method reaches 54.3 mIoU versus LUDVIG’s 50.4, and the supplementary runtime breakdown reports approximately 9.25 minutes for semantic processing of an already reconstructed scene.

The ablations support specific components: VLM-generated text improves LERF mIoU from 50.1 with filtered image-feature aggregation to 54.3, while combined neutral-point filtering improves the unfiltered result from 53.0 to 54.3.
The supplement supplies useful implementation details, including the VLM prompt, tracking parameters, matching threshold, model alternatives, runtime breakdown, and qualitative failure cases.
weaknesses: The efficiency comparison does not fully establish a central claimed advantage. Table 1 measures CLIP-feature storage rather than total semantic storage, omitting explicit accounting for overlapping Gaussian membership indices. It also lists training time rather than comparable complete adaptation time. The local VRAM and runtime measurements do not explain how Gemini inference resources, latency, and cost are accounted for. Consequently, the claimed orders-of-magnitude reduction in total overhead is insufficiently substantiated.

The contribution of the proposed representation is not adequately isolated. There is no single-granularity versus overlapping-group ablation, nor a controlled comparison that equips an existing grouping approach with the same tracker and VLM descriptions. Table 5 supports text distillation, but cannot establish that geometry–semantics decoupling itself explains the gains. The relationship to cited grouping and mask-lifting approaches, including FlashSplat and Segment-then-Splat, also needs more precise technical differentiation.

The LERF state-of-the-art claim contradicts Table 2. The reported 54.3 mean is below LAGA’s 64.0, 3DVLGS’s 62.0, and Occam’s LGS’s 61.3; the stated 3.9-point improvement applies to LUDVIG. Strongest benchmark performance is not necessary for acceptance, but this distinction materially changes the claimed empirical contribution.

Neutral-point processing contains an implementation-relevant inconsistency. Section 3.3 retains high-entropy points when their opacity exceeds the opacity threshold; thus setting that threshold to zero should retain essentially all positive-opacity candidates. Appendix 7.2 instead describes this setting as removing all high-entropy points. Moreover, entropy and opacity establish a useful filtering heuristic, but do not demonstrate that the removed points inherently lack semantic identity.

The five-noun representation is evaluated mainly through object/category queries, leaving the broader claims of rich polysemy and nuanced open-vocabulary understanding incompletely supported. Attribute and relational information can be lost during noun generation. The CLIP checkpoint, query-threshold sensitivity, and handling of overlapping class predictions in ScanNet are also insufficiently specified.

Overall, the measured segmentation gains and practical representation place this near the acceptance boundary. The unresolved efficiency accounting and limited isolation of the central architectural contribution prevent a clear acceptance recommendation; these are more consequential than the correctable wording and presentation issues.

strengths: ExtrinSplat offers a useful, understandable design: overlapping Gaussian groups linked to object-level text embeddings support direct 3D selection without per-scene semantic optimization. Separating semantic indexing from geometry is practically attractive for querying and editing.

ScanNet results are strong within the evaluated ten-scene protocol. Table 3 reports 45.5 mIoU for 19 classes versus 40.7 for InstanceGaussian, with improvements also present for the 15- and 10-class settings.

The LERF result demonstrates competitive training-free performance: 54.3 mIoU versus LUDVIG’s 50.4. Table 5 supports the benefit of VLM text distillation over the strongest tested image-feature aggregation variant, which achieves 50.1.

The manuscript provides useful implementation details, component timings, failure examples, and several ablations. Combining entropy and opacity filtering improves LERF mIoU from 53.0 to 54.3, while the supplementary experiments examine VLM choice, descriptor count, and threshold sensitivity.
weaknesses: The LERF state-of-the-art claim contradicts Table 2. ExtrinSplat’s 54.3 mean trails LAGA’s 64.0, 3DVLGS’s 62.0, and Occam’s LGS’s 61.3. The claimed 3.9-point improvement applies to LUDVIG, not the strongest listed method. Benchmark leadership is unnecessary for this contribution, but the distinction materially changes the interpretation of the results.

The efficiency comparisons do not establish the claimed total resource savings. Table 1 measures CLIP feature storage rather than the complete semantic representation, omitting explicit accounting for overlapping group memberships and compressed baseline representations. Table 9 includes VLM latency, but attributing all timings to a single V100 does not explain Gemini’s remote compute or costs. Comparing semantic adaptation time against InstanceGaussian’s Gaussian training time also requires a clearly matched accounting boundary.

The central architectural claims are insufficiently isolated. There is no ablation of overlapping versus exclusive groups or multi-granularity versus single-granularity grouping. Table 5 supports replacing CLIP image features with VLM-generated text, but does not establish how much improvement follows from the proposed extrinsic representation itself. The novelty relative to existing grouping and segment-then-splat approaches needs more precise technical differentiation.

Neutral-point processing contains a reproducibility-relevant contradiction. Section 3.3 retains high-entropy points when opacity exceeds the threshold, so setting the opacity threshold to zero should retain essentially all positive-opacity candidates. The supplement instead says this setting removes all high-entropy points and reports the entropy-only result. Moreover, low opacity and cross-view disagreement are plausible heuristics, but do not establish that identified points intrinsically lack semantic identity.

The claimed breadth of semantic understanding exceeds the evidence. Five generated nouns create a semantic bottleneck whose ability to preserve attributes, relations, and unusual descriptions is not systematically tested. The reported dependence on VLM choice—47.0 to 54.3 mIoU—also makes model configuration and repeatability important. The manuscript does not clearly specify the CLIP checkpoint, VLM generation settings, or how conflicting class predictions from overlapping groups are resolved for ScanNet.

Overall, the strong ScanNet results and practical pipeline place the paper near acceptance, but uncertainties in resource accounting, attribution of the central contributions, and implementation consistency prevent a stronger recommendation. These concerns extend beyond presentation refinements; the incorrect LERF headline alone would not justify rejection.
